rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds with low risk of truncation while spreading retention across the window. This first run should reveal the overall elution range and whether selectivity or speed is the main limitation.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to reduce t_last below 10 min by steepening the gradient while holding selectivity constant. A moderate cut in tG should test how much runtime can be recovered before the tightest cluster around peaks 5–7 starts to lose resolution.

The current method is nearly ideal and the limiting pair is just above threshold, so the next step is a small further reduction in tG to try to bring t_last under 10 min. This probes whether we can gain the remaining time without pushing the 6/7 pair below Rs 1.5.

At tG 14 min the only issue is the 6/7 pair, so keep the fast gradient and adjust selectivity with a small temperature decrease. Lowering T often increases retention and can change selectivity enough to recover that borderline pair while hopefully keeping t_last under 10 min.

Lower temperature hurt selectivity badly, so test the opposite direction at the same fast gradient to see whether a small increase in T improves the critical cluster around peaks 5–7. This directly probes whether temperature can rescue full resolution at tG 14 min while preserving the sub-10 min last peak.

Higher temperature at tG 14 worsened the critical pair, but it also shortened the run, so combine that temperature with a slightly shallower gradient to see if Rs can be restored while still keeping t_last near or below 10 min. This explores whether the optimum lies on a time/selectivity tradeoff ridge rather than exactly at 40 C.

Since temperature changes degraded the critical cluster, try altering late-gradient strength instead while keeping the fast 14 min program. Lowering phi1 slightly should mostly affect the late strong-solvent region, potentially increasing selectivity for the crowded mid-eluters without much penalty to the already acceptable t_last.

Dropping phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6/7 pair while keeping t_last under 10 min, so continue one more step in the same direction. This should reveal whether a slightly weaker final solvent is enough to push that pair to full credit without sacrificing the time term.

The key challenge is still the 6/7 pair near the threshold, so keep the faster 12 min gradient and test whether a small temperature decrease at phi1 0.90 can improve selectivity enough to recover resolution while staying under 10 min. Since lowering temperature strongly worsened selectivity, test the opposite direction at the same 12 min and phi1 0.90 settings. This checks whether higher temperature can improve the critical cluster enough to beat the current best while retaining the sub-10 min analysis time.

The best region appears to be around phi1 0.85–0.90 at 40 C, and phi1 0.85 gave full resolution but only a small time penalty at 14 min. Increasing tG to 16 min there should map the slope–resolution tradeoff more completely and may reveal a more robust fully resolved method with only a modest CRF loss relative to the current best.

The best method is very close to full credit, so we should keep exploring selectivity around that exact phi1/tG combination. Testing 45 C at the current best composition will show whether temperature gives a favorable selectivity shift there, despite being harmful at steeper gradients.

Temperature is clearly not helping, so probe a different lever by raising phi0 while keeping the best phi1, tG, and T. A slightly narrower gradient window may shift the crowded middle of the chromatogram enough to improve the 6/7 pair while potentially shortening the run further.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved both runtime and the critical 6/7 pair, so continue one more step in that direction while keeping the rest fixed. This is the most promising route to push the last sub-threshold pair over Rs 1.5 without giving up the zero time penalty.

The best improvement came from increasing phi0, and lowering phi1 previously improved the critical 6/7 pair, so combine those two favorable changes. This has a strong chance of pushing the last pair to full resolution, though we need to check whether t_last stays close enough to 10 min.

We have reached full CRF, so the only remaining objective is to see whether the method can be made faster before resolution drops below 1.5. Shortening tG by one step from the winning conditions is the cleanest way to test the edge, with the expectation that we can revert if the critical 6/7 pair fails.

Testing phi0 0.15 with the winning phi1 and tG checks whether we can retain full resolution with a bit more speed, potentially finding another CRF 1.000 method with shorter t_last.

We already have CRF 1.000, so the only worthwhile search is for an equally perfect but faster method. Since increasing phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 kept full resolution and reduced t_last, one more step upward is the most promising boundary test before resolution starts to fail.

The phi0 0.15, phi1 0.85, tG 14 method is already perfect, so test a slightly lower phi1 from that strong starting point to see if full resolution can be maintained with improved selectivity and possibly similar or better practical robustness. This is a focused boundary check around the current optimum family.
